stories.title: Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review
stories.summary: An engrossing expansion full of interesting new characters and vibrant enemies.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review
sources.text: The first Dark Arisen expansion for the original Dragon’s Dogma has a well-lauded place in video game history as the expansion that “fixed” the base game, sanding down the rough technical edges and tweaking things to make the notoriously obtuse RPG more approachable. It also added hours of new content, spiraling an already heady story directly into the heavens on the back of dragon wings. Dark Arisen 2 isn’t as transformational as the first one was, primarily because many of Dragon’s Dogma 2’s biggest issues have been fixed through incremental patching since it came out in 2024. But the new content here definitely flies in the same ambitious skies as its predecessor, pushing the story and world design to new heights, even if some of the new progression options get left behind. As with Dragon’s Dogma 2’s base campaign, Dark Arisen 2’s story remixes themes from the first game without being a simple retelling. Like in the first, another Arisen has been rumored to exist, something that shouldn’t be possible and demands your immediate attention. This takes you north to the frozen mountains of Norgan, a place that is largely abandoned save for the single settlement at its border (and the steady stream of visitors coming from other lands to investigate what’s been lost under all that ice besides you). The expansion’s story also meanders in similar ways to the base game, with plot points getting sidetracked by little tasks or other happenings, but it didn’t feel as distracting since a lot of the “help me and I’ll help you” quests are relegated to side stories. As a whole, this roughly 20-hour main quest is solid, lacking in nuanced writing or ground breaking storytelling but bursting with a tangibly broody mood, big moments, and some genuinely interesting lore. It’s meditation on how a hero of destiny chooses their fate (if they get a choice at all) is unsubtle, and spends far too long at the end really sending the message home, but it sticks it. For those who don’t mind a lot of filler with their killer, there are plenty of people with tasks thoroughly less vital to the survival of reality that need doing. A couple of those quest lines stand out – one where you help the son of the village’s leader become brave and tough enough to follow in his footsteps, for example – but most are just a flimsy excuse to run around the world and beat up enemies. The frigid Norgan region is delightfully dense with things to find and see even if its smaller than most other regions in Dragon’s Dogma 2. What it lacks in square footage on a map, it gains in a sprawling sense of height that stretches from it’s jagged icy peaks down to winding underground caverns that spread wide and interconnect. Navigating up and down the rocks is a treacherous and daunting road at first, but climbing hooks can be used on specific poles scattered throughout to bridge elevations without the fuss. Combined with how dungeons and caves tended to loop back on themselves, revealing exits or opening doors that served as their own shortcuts into and out of zones, and Dark Arisen 2 felt almost like a Zelda or Metroid game in ways this series never has before. The abundance of portcrystals scattered around the map is another navigational relief. There are more in Norgan than there are in Vermund and Bathall combined, making travelling to different zones far more reasonable than it was in the base game. Note that reasonable doesn’t necessarily mean easier. The portcrystal’s abundance is a practical matter, as ox carts wouldn’t last long in the harsh environments. Norgan’s wintry winds often pick up, turning snowfall into blinding whiteouts that threaten to freeze you to death if you aren’t protected by special winterized gear or new consumables designed to stave off these frost effects for a limited time. These came in abundance pretty regularly so I never felt like my life was in danger out there, but the scrambling effect it has on the minimap and how generally hard it is to see or navigate in real time made them a threat worth waiting out at camp. Norgan’s crumbling castles and snowcapped cliffs are a welcome change of pace from the rolling hills and dense hinterlands of Vermund and he craggy deserts of Bathall. It’s also not all snowy wastes. I was surprised to see a break in the snow drifts when I came across a festering poisonous swamp. It matches thematically in that everything in it is dead (or maybe wishes it was), but areas like that and the crystal caves deep below the mountains subverted my expectations for the region in a welcome way. The bulk of what you’ll find hidden in the snow are Spoils, a new gear type that appears in generic shapes (long weapon, aegis, etc.) at first, but is revealed to be a usable piece of equipment when appraised by one of the new NPCs. Rolling the dice for new gear was not particularly exciting, and it further isolated me from having any real attachment to my equipment in a game that already had an abundance of junk to constantly ignore. There are at least things outside of raw stats to consider, as each piece of gear can potentially have special attributes that grant passive abilities or enhance specific weapon skills – but no single piece of gear stayed in rotation long enough to be something I relied on much, with the deluge of experience points I received strapping a rocket to my leveling almost immediately. I can see how these could fit into an endgame grind, but participating in a lottery in hopes to get incrementally stronger as my levels reaches the mid 100s is the sort of loop that I, like The Arisen, simply don’t have the heart for. New skills and abilities for every vocation can be learned from obelisks that dot the ridges and tundra in Norgan. Each have multiple tiers of offerings, and while the first are available for purchase with rift points immediately, the rest need to be unlocked with offering flames, earned in Dark Arisen 2’s second big campaign: the repeatable 12 Lost Rites dungeons

sources.title: Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen review: um RPG completo e com muitos detalhes na jogabilidade
sources.text: Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen vale a pena para quem gosta de RPG de mundo aberto com sistemas profundos, peões com personalidade própria e horas e mais horas de exploração, e o preço compensa pela quantidade de conteúdo. Mas se você espera gráficos ultrarrealistas, uma história cheia de reviravoltas ou um jogo que explica tudo de mão beijada, prepare-se: aqui o tempo (o seu e o do jogo) é parte da experiência. Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen é a versão completa do RPG de ação da Capcom lançado em 2024, agora acompanhado de uma expansão inédita ambientada na região de Norgan. O pacote chega em 9 de outubro de 2026 para PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC (Steam) e, pela primeira vez, Nintendo Switch 2, plataforma em que testei o jogo. O primeiro Dragon’s Dogma, de 20212, chegou ao PlayStation 3 e ao Xbox 360 em maio daquele ano, dirigido por Hideaki Itsuno, nome que os fãs de ação conhecem de Devil May Cry . A história começa em Cassardis, uma vila de pescadores no ducado de Gransys, quando um dragão ataca, arranca o coração do protagonista e o deixa vivo. A partir dali, você se torna o Arisen, o escolhido destinado a enfrentar a criatura. A grande sacada do jogo, já naquela época, eram os peões: companheiros controlados pela inteligência artificial que você cria, treina e compartilha com outros jogadores. Um peão seu podia acompanhar a aventura de outra pessoa e voltar com conhecimento novo sobre missões e inimigos. Em abril de 2013, a Capcom lançou Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen , uma versão expandida que juntava o jogo original a um conteúdo novo e bem mais difícil: a Bitterblack Isle, uma ilha-masmorra pensada para o pós-jogo. Foi essa edição que manteve a franquia viva por anos, ganhando versões para PC em 2016, PS4 e Xbox One em 2017 e Nintendo Switch em 2019. No meio do caminho, o Japão recebeu ainda o Dragon’s Dogma Online (2015), um spin-off online que nunca saiu de lá e foi encerrado em 2019, e a Netflix lançou uma adaptação em anime em 2020. A sequência demorou mais de uma década para chegar. Dragon’s Dogma 2 foi lançado em 22 de março de 2024 para PS5, Xbox Series X|S e PC. Nele, você volta a ser o Arisen, mas desperta sem memória, enquanto um impostor ocupa o trono do reino de Vermund. O mapa se divide entre Vermund, terra dos humanos, e Battahl, lar dos beastren. O jogo passou de 4 milhões de cópias vendidas até o fim de 2025 sem receber nenhuma expansão, uma lacuna que finalmente foi preenchida agora. Assim como em 2013, o novo Dark Arisen junta o jogo-base a um conteúdo inédito, e não por acaso: a expansão é dirigida por Kento Kinoshita, o mesmo diretor do Dark Arisen original. Segundo a Capcom , a nova campanha leva o Arisen ao norte, para Norgan, uma região gelada abandonada há muito tempo. Lá, ele encontra o Dragão Caído (Fallen Dragon), uma criatura imortal que está sem o próprio coração, e se une a uma personagem misteriosa chamada Eir para investigar os segredos dela. O espelho com o primeiro jogo é claro: se antes era o Arisen quem perdia o coração para um dragão, agora é o dragão quem vaga sem ele. Além da campanha, a expansão traz 12 masmorras de desafio, chamadas Lost Rites, que recompensam com equipamentos raros, e relíquias encontradas na exploração de Norgan, que podem ser avaliadas por NPCs específicos para forjar armas e armaduras mais fortes, algumas com efeitos e habilidades únicas. O editor de personagens também ganhou novos penteados e tatuagens. O visual de Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen não é nada impressionante no Nintendo Switch 2. É o padrão de um RPG desse porte, em que o que importa mais é a mecânica e a história do que gráficos extremamente avançados. Quem chega esperando um espetáculo visual de nova geração vai se decepcionar, mas quem conhece a proposta da série sabe que o foco nunca esteve aí. As cutscenes, por outro lado, são bem feitas e cumprem bem o papel de dar peso aos momentos da história. Joguei no Nintendo Switch 2, no modo portátil, com todas as configurações no máximo. O jogo roda a no máximo 30 FPS, com o FSR 3 Frame Generation ligado. A Capcom confirmou que essa é a primeira vez que usa geração de quadros num jogo de Switch 2: o recurso interpola imagens para chegar a algo equivalente a 60 FPS, e pode ser ligado ou desligado a qualquer momento. Durante a jogatina em si, não percebi travamentos ou dificuldades. O único ponto que me incomodou foram algumas cutscenes que demoraram a entrar, dando a impressão de que o console precisava de mais tempo para carregá-las. O mundo de Dragon’s Dogma 2 é aberto, e você vai aceitando diversas missões ao longo da jornada. E aqui vai o primeiro conselho: cuidado para não acumular missões demais e esquecer as que dependem do tempo. Um exemplo: ao chegar a Vernworth, a capital de Vermund, recebi uma missão para entrar no castelo e encontrar uma pessoa. Só que isso só era para ser feito à meia-noite. Não existe um relógio na tela marcando o prazo, mas também não dá para enrolar e esperar o dia raiar. Essa passagem de tempo influencia diversas situações. Pessoas que ficam num lugar durante o dia podem estar em outro à noite. Para avançar as horas, você pode se hospedar numa pousada ou usar bancos especiais espalhados por alguns locais. A noite tem regras próprias. Você precisa de uma lamparina para enxergar no escuro, o que também ajuda a localizar – e ser localizado pelo – os monstros, e, nas áreas selvagens, encontra criaturas diferentes das que aparecem durante o dia. Até os itens sentem o tempo passar. Uma maçã, por exemplo, pode amadurecer, envelhecer e virar itens diferentes para a combinação de materiais. Os alimentos crus pedem atenção redobrada, para que você não acabe consumindo algo velho ou podre que traga efeitos colaterais. Essa foi a parte em que achei a explicação do jogo mais fraca. Há uma variedade enorme de itens, e você acaba tendo que fazer combinações na sorte para descobrir novos objetos. stories.title: Muramasa: Revenant Blades has 108 swords, and its definitive update for PC wants to make sure you use them all
stories.summary: The swords may be cursed, but the action is better than ever.

sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: Muramasa: Revenant Blades has 108 swords, and its definitive update for PC wants to make sure you use them all
sources.text: The swords may be cursed, but the action is better than ever. The Japanese Sword Museum in Tokyo, set along the bank of the Sumida river, enshrines behind glass a collection of remarkable blades spanning hundreds of years of craftsmanship. Books about the longer uchigatana and shorter wakizashi, some of them written by the museum's very donors, celebrate the swordsmiths who hammered them out of steel. But flip through one, and there's a good chance you won't spot the name Muramasa, despite his swords playing a prominent role in some of Japan's most famous battles. Centuries of mythology building up around the idea that your swords were cursed will tend to do that to a guy. Vanillaware's Muramasa: Revenant Blades, at least, isn't afraid to lean into the legacy. The 2D action game is so in love with swords it's got 108 of them, and it turns the superstition that Muramasa's swords had to taste blood once unsheathed into a simple but enticing mechanic: Each comes with a unique skill, which can be equipped on another sword only after it's had its fill of bloodshed. "There's definitely this reputation that the swords of Muramasa are cursed, but what that means is they have power," says director Wataru Nakanishi. "In this game Muramasa is an important character and will create these very powerful swords, but in turn [the protagonists] must collect souls for him, so they have this cooperative relationship based around this dark situation." In a way Revenant Blades is lifting a curse of its own: 17 years after the game was first released on the Nintendo Wii as Muramasa: The Demon Blade, it's somehow the first release from Vanillaware to make it to PC. The Japanese studio followed Muramasa with more nuanced games, like 2019's acclaimed 13 Sentinels: Aegis Rim and 2024 tactics RPG Unicorn Overlord, but after playing Muramasa on PC I can see why the studio started here. I remember a hack-and-slash with art so lavish seeming novel back in 2009, and somehow that's just as true today. The painterly art has a timeless quality to it, though that's something of an illusion. "It was a lot of work, and it was very difficult," Nakanishi said, laughing. "We had some of the assets, but not others. For those we had to pull them from the game, and then artists individually by hand had to touch them up and recreate them to make something appropriate for the HD release. But you know, through that arduous hand-drawn process, we were able to create this warm and colorful art that we think people will be happy to see." Revenant Blades is also not the simplistic game I remember. The skill system for all 108 blades is new, allowing me to equip three ground and three air abilities to a trio of blades I could have equipped (and swap between) at any one time. That made for a dizzying number of special moves to keep in mind, though executing them is as simple as tapping a button and a direction. Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. On the harder difficulty enemies now come streaming onto the screen in daunting numbers, and with more health to compensate for your improved arsenal. I learned the hard way not to play too defensively: Blocking a few attacks would wear down my sword until it snapped, leaving me open to a quick death. Survival demands fluid strings of combos, flitting between swords to keep them from breaking, chaining a launcher skill into a rapid series of slashes that can pummel a whole gang of ninja at once. Or toads. I walked underneath a waterfall, not realizing I was underleveled for that bit of Muramasa's freely explorable map, and got absolutely embarrassed by a family of poison-spitting toads. Way scarier than the guys with shurikens and bombs. In the original game enemies scaled with you as you leveled up, but Vanillaware scrapped that for Revenant Blades. Enemies in different areas now have fixed levels; you'll be able to steamroll the ones that are weaker than you, but depending on the path you take you might run into fights that send you scampering away unless you're really good. Because you could previously only use a single skill that was locked to the single katana you had in-hand at any given moment, Nakanishi says players naturally gravitated to the most powerful late-game blades. "It kind of limited the scope of the gameplay," he says, but now that you can equip skills independently, "players have access to so many more skills and playstyles." "Using the skills Celestial Slash and Flame Barrage, you can knock people into the air with fire, then jump up and use the aerial skill to knock them back to the ground. That kind of combination wasn't really something you could do with the more limited skill system." In addition to possessed princess Momohime who I played as for the hour-long demo, Revenant Blades piles on a range of playable characters first added in a 2013 Vita re-release, each with their own stories. It's now a deceptively beefy game, and the skill system feels like the key it needed to unlock its full potential. I can't imagine a better fit for the Steam Deck OLED, where its vivid backgrounds will threaten to tear the eyes away from the action for the three seconds it'll take to wind up dead. If Muramasa: Revenant Blades is the hit on PC it deserves to be, perhaps it will manage to dispel the myth that PC ports are as taboo in the halls of Vanillaware as the swordsmith's weapons have become over the centuries. Could more follow in its wake? "We currently don't have any specific plans of that nature, but we would love to see Muramasa be successful enough that people start to ask about that kind of thing," Nakanishi says. 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together Wes has been covering games and hardware for more than 10 years, first at tech sites like The Wirecutter

sources.title: Muramasa: Revenant Blades hands-on gameplay preview
sources.text: Recently, I had the chance to visit Marvelous at its Shinagawa headquarters for a one-hour preview of its upcoming Vanillaware side-scrolling action RPG remaster Muramasa: Revenant Blades . As a disclaimer, attendees were gifted a special wooden box engraved with the Muramasa logo, containing a themed bottle of sake. Going into this preview, I should mention that I have not played any previous Vanillaware titles—including Muramasa: The Demon Blade for Wii or Muramasa Rebirth for PS Vita —so I cannot offer direct comparisons to prior versions. The full game will feature six playable characters, though the demo restricted us to one of the original two: Kisuke or Momohime. Of the two available difficulty settings, I opted for Momohime on the higher difficulty. I started by testing out the controls to get a feel for the movement mechanics, like checking whether holding the jump button versus tapping it altered jump height (it does not!), or if mid-air direction changes were possible (they are!). The demo starts out pretty simple: you run to the right and dispatch enemies in your path, much like an 8- or 16-bit side-scroller. Some encounters lock the screen until every enemy is defeated, while later areas allow you to run past enemies entirely. Combat feels fluid, with various movement options and abilities. You can dash, dodge, jump, and execute combo strings both on the ground and in mid-air. Additionally, each weapon has its own special, super-style move. Most enemies encountered during my one-hour session were easy enough to manage with basic attack strings and light dodging. Later on, however, straw-hat samurai enemies appear that require blocking to defeat. While relying solely on spamming the attack button would make the game too repetitive, having to stop and wait for enemy strikes to block did slow down the pacing of battle. Veterans of the series may be able to confirm if additional techniques unlock later to deal with these foes faster. Control-wise, the inputs for blocking and jumping felt close enough that I occasionally jumped by mistake, which led to my untimely doom on a few occasions. I also encountered a boss named “Blue Monk,” but being an early-game encounter, he did not put up much resistance. Notably, you can land hits continuously—unlike some games that only let you get in a certain number of hits before the boss gains invincibility frames until they “recover.” Weapons lose durability as you fight, dealing reduced damage as they degrade and requiring you to swap between weapons. Switching between equipped weapons and using items via quick button prompts feels smooth and responsive. Personally, I would prefer mechanics that incentivize weapon swapping for positive reasons—such as using certain abilities or unique weapon-switch-related combos—rather than forcing a switch through damage penalties. Without added combat perks for swapping, the mechanic feels less like an engaging feature and more like a distraction during intense fights, where your focus is split until you realize your reduced damage demands a switch. After a fairly linear start, the game opens up into multiple branching paths, much like a Metroidvania. Environments include villages, caves, and beaches. A map can be used to find your way around, filling in areas as you visit them, and complete with an objective icon guiding you to the next main objective. Near the end of my time with the demo, I rushed ahead to see how far I could get before time expired. I stumbled into a maybe-winnable battle against a horde of straw-hat samurai enemies, while entirely out of healing items and resources. While grinding does not seem strictly necessary in this game, fighting basic enemies to stockpile resources before tough battles is definitely helpful. That said, players with sufficient skill should be able to push through most mandatory fights regardless. While I reiterate that I have not played any of the previous releases, certain additions are notable, like the ability to master a weapon skill and equip it independently of the weapon itself. Overall, the game controls intuitively and feels smooth to play. While the art style isn’t personally my preference, I encountered no bugs or major technical issues. Fans of the genre, and of Muramasa —a game locked to platforms that are no longer very easily accessible—will likely find a lot to enjoy here. Muramasa: Revenant Blades is due out for PlayStation 5 , Switch 2 , Switch , and PC via Steam on February 4, 2027. View a new set of screenshots at the gallery .

sources.title: How The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival Builds a Tactical Brawler
sources.text: Hello everyone. The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC, and rather than walk you through a feature list, I wanted to talk about the decisions that went into creating it. AMC’s “The Walking Dead” is a world defined by scarcity, tension, and the consequences of every decision. The “All Out War” arc adds another dimension to that foundation: momentum, escalation, and increasingly intense confrontations as the conflict with the Saviors grows. Streets of Survival brings those qualities together through a blend of exploration, resource management, and arcade-inspired brawler combat. Search your surroundings, gather supplies and information, and decide how best to approach the dangers ahead. When conflict erupts, combat delivers the immediacy and intensity the story demands, while keeping every encounter grounded in a larger purpose. You are not simply clearing rooms or fighting toward a score screen. Every confrontation moves you closer to an objective, a character, or a reckoning with the Saviors. Exploration creates tension, resources give decisions weight, and combat provides the payoff, combining into an experience built around the escalating conflict at the heart of The Walking Dead’s All Out War. Rick, Daryl and Michonne are not three skins over one moveset. Each has a signature weapon, a separate set of animations and their own skill tree that you invest in every level, which means the same encounter requires a different strategy depending on the selected character. Rick relies on his magnum: long-range firepower that turns every fight into an ammo-management problem. Michonne thrives in close quarters, cutting through hordes with her katana and rewarding you for staying inside the danger. Daryl uses his crossbow to thin threats from a distance before diving in to finish the rest, which makes him the most positional of the three. The levels are tailored around the character meant to play them, creating an experience that adjusts to that character’s available weapons and abilities and giving more freedom in the design, while delivering a custom puzzle for players to solve in each situation. The second big design decision was to stop treating enemies as one mass enemy. Walkers are pressure. They overwhelm through volume and they punish anyone who stands still. The Saviors are opposition: they block, they fire from a distance, and they will happily use walker hordes as cover while they line up a shot. Because both are on screen at once, you are never solving a single problem. That separation exists to change the verb of the combat. In a classic brawler the verb is clear. Here I wanted it to be control: funnel the walkers into a narrow path, isolate the Saviors before they regroup, and save the ammo you’ll need for the targets that actually call for it. The environments are part of that same system rather than a backdrop. Each rewards a different approach, and each one can be turned into a weapon or cost you a health bar if you move through it carelessly. Face enemies between them, lure them into more favorable positions to fight, or use your surroundings in your favor. Giving you different approaches to the same situations was an exciting challenge. Reaching the end credits is where the second design pass starts paying off, as you now have the option to play levels with any character, including the unlockable Negan. Each playable character’s skill tree branches, so a second run with the same survivor is a different build, and playing the same level with a different survivor creates a totally different game. The higher difficulty settings are not damage multipliers: they turn chaotic encounters into tactical puzzles where positioning is the only thing that keeps you alive. Whether you’re returning with a different survivor, experimenting with a new skill path or pushing into higher difficulties, the goal is for every run to ask you to approach the apocalypse differently. The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC.

sources.text: Hoje marca o lançamento mundial de Gears of War: E-Day , já disponível no XBOX Series X|S, XBOX no PC, Game Pass e Steam. Uma das sagas mais icônicas de XBOX retorna ao ponto onde tudo começou, levando os jogadores de volta às primeiras horas do Dia da Emergência e ao evento catastrófico que mudou para sempre o mundo de Sera. Gears of War: E-Day nos transporta de volta às primeiras horas da invasão Locust, quando um mundo desprevenido é brutalmente lançado no caos à medida que monstros emergem do subsolo. Ao longo de três dias e noites angustiantes, Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago e seus destemidos novos companheiros de esquadrão lutam desesperadamente para sobreviver ao ataque que consome a cidade de Kalona, enquanto descobrem a verdadeira dimensão de uma ameaça diferente de tudo o que eles — ou a humanidade — já enfrentaram. Desde o início do prólogo, Gears of War: E-Day oferece uma verdadeira aula de ação e terror. Este não é o inimigo Locust que você já enfrentou antes. Eles são tão astutos quanto violentos e, francamente, você deveria ter medo de encará-los. Seja esta a sua primeira missão ou o seu retorno da aposentadoria para lutar na guerra que está por vir, nós ajudamos você a se preparar. Antes de sair pelas ruas de Kalona, confira algumas dicas que todo Gear precisa saber. 1 – Saiba quando se movimentar ou sair da p**ra do caminho Gears of War é conhecido por ser um jogo de tiro por cobertura, e você dependerá dela para continuar vivo enquanto avança contra os Locust. Mantenha a cabeça baixa, mova-se de uma cobertura para outra e evite sair em campo aberto, a menos que esteja partindo para cima de um inimigo com um ataque corpo a corpo. Mesmo um pequeno grupo de Drones pode causar um dano enorme enquanto você estiver exposto, o que pode trazer problemas tanto para você quanto para o companheiro de esquadrão que talvez precise vir reanimá-lo. Às vezes, a melhor opção é manter a posição com paciência e eliminar os inimigos conforme eles se aproximam — e não há vergonha alguma nessa estratégia. Em outros momentos, você simplesmente precisará correr com tudo e se manter o mais móvel possível — algo que aprendi rapidamente durante um confronto inicial com um Brumak empunhando uma terrível arma de corrente. Nessa situação, não há segurança atrás de uma cobertura: espalhem-se, mantenham a criatura distraída e torçam para que ela não decida investir contra você enquanto sua arma estiver emperrada. Cada arma que você encontrará em E-Day é mais adequada a determinadas situações, o que proporciona uma ótima experiência tática. A Lancer com Motosserra é uma excelente opção versátil, oferecendo poder de fogo a curta e média distância e um carregador enorme — que pode ser aprimorado — para você esvaziar. A Gnasher é uma escopeta excepcional, perfeita para causar dano devastador à queima-roupa. O rifle de precisão Longshot , um dos meus favoritos, dispara projéteis potentes e precisos contra inimigos desavisados a grandes distâncias. Além de ser extremamente satisfatório todas as vezes, isso permite causar uma boa quantidade de dano a inimigos mais resistentes — como um Boomer — antes que eles se aproximem. Também há depósitos espalhados por Kalona que permitem alterar seu conjunto de armas, então não pense que ficará preso para sempre a um estilo específico de jogo. Varie sua estratégia, troque de função com seus amigos e, acima de tudo, experimente! 3 – Combate corpo a corpo é o melhor amigo de um Gear Eu sei que disse que este é um jogo de tiro por cobertura, mas, às vezes, você precisará recorrer a medidas mais pessoais. Antes mesmo de E-Day permitir que você encoste em uma arma, o jogo oferece um curso intensivo de combate corpo a corpo — uma das habilidades mais úteis e capazes de salvar a vida de um Gear. Dedique algum tempo para entender como esse sistema funciona ao empunhar um cano de metal e a pistola Snub: sinta o peso do golpe e como é atingir inimigos à sua frente e, mais importante, atrás de você. Mais adiante, o combate corpo a corpo fica ainda mais divertido com a Lancer com Motosserra, e você se sentirá muito mais confiante ao usá-la depois de dominar os fundamentos dos golpes. 4 – Atirar sem mirar está de volta e continua eficaz Assim que você coloca a cabeça para fora para mirar, transforma-se em um verdadeiro ímã de balas, praticamente convidando todos os inimigos armados no mapa a estourá-lo como um balão. Felizmente, os Gears podem atirar sem mirar por trás da cobertura, uma excelente maneira de causar dano adicional a algo que esteja se aproximando demais. Se você não tiver vida suficiente para avançar e realizar uma finalização corpo a corpo, ou precisar de alguns segundos para se recuperar, atirar sem mirar a partir da cobertura pode ser a jogada decisiva para dar conta do recado. 5 – Fique de olho em missões paralelas e suas recompensas Embora a campanha de E-Day seja predominantemente linear, Kalona conta com grandes áreas abertas que oferecem vários caminhos até o próximo objetivo, além de rotas alternativas que podem levar a missões paralelas. Esses são objetivos menores e opcionais que permitem apoiar outros esquadrões, ajudar civis e contribuir de outras formas para salvar a cidade. Além de oferecerem mais contexto sobre a história como um todo, essas missões também rendem boas recompensas, geralmente uma modificação de arma. 6 – Um sinal sonoro indica itens colecionáveis Enquanto explora, fique atento a um som agudo sempre que entrar em uma nova área da cidade — seja dentro de um edifício ou em uma rua lateral. Isso significa que há um item colecionável por perto. Eles variam de itens conhecidos, como armaduras e identificações da CGO, a objetos inusitados, como… uma lata de sopa. Todos também incluem ótimos pequenos registros de história, alguns escritos pelos próprios integrantes do esquadrão.
